stem: The 'distribution of population' refers to __________.
options: The way in which people are spread across the Earth's surface (where people live and where they do not)
The total number of people in the world
The rate at which population grows
solution: The DISTRIBUTION of POPULATION refers to the WAY in which PEOPLE are SPREAD across the Earth's surface — i.e., WHERE people live and where they do NOT. Population is very UNEVENLY distributed: some regions (like South and East Asia) are densely populated, while others (deserts, high mountains, dense forests, polar regions) are sparsely populated. Understanding this spatial pattern of where people live is the study of population distribution. So distribution refers to the spatial spread of people. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Population density' is defined as __________.
options: The number of persons per unit area (e.g., persons per square kilometre)
The total population of a country
solution: POPULATION DENSITY is defined as the NUMBER of PERSONS per UNIT AREA — usually expressed as persons per SQUARE KILOMETRE (or per square mile). It is calculated by dividing the total population of an area by its land area. Density measures how crowded or sparsely settled an area is, allowing comparison between regions. (This is the 'arithmetic' density; other measures like physiological density also exist.) So density is the number of persons per unit area. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The distribution of world population is HIGHLY __________.
options: Uneven (a small part of the Earth's surface holds a large share of the population, while vast areas are sparsely populated)
solution: The distribution of world population is HIGHLY UNEVEN. A SMALL part of the Earth's surface holds a LARGE SHARE of the world's people (about 90% of the world's population lives on roughly 10% of the land), while VAST AREAS — deserts, high mountains, dense forests, and cold polar regions — are very SPARSELY populated or almost empty. A few regions (like South Asia, East Asia, and parts of Europe) are extremely densely populated. So world population distribution is highly uneven. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The regions with the highest concentrations of world population include __________.
options: South and East Asia (e.g., India, China), Europe, and north-eastern USA
The Amazon rainforest and the Arctic
The Himalayas and the Gobi Desert
solution: The regions with the HIGHEST CONCENTRATIONS of world population include: SOUTH ASIA (e.g., INDIA, Pakistan, Bangladesh) and EAST ASIA (e.g., CHINA, Japan); EUROPE (especially western/central Europe); and the north-eastern USA. These densely populated areas generally have favourable conditions — fertile plains and river valleys, moderate climates, water availability, and industrial/economic development. (In contrast, deserts, dense forests, high mountains, and polar regions are sparsely populated.) So the highest concentrations are in South/East Asia, Europe, and north-eastern USA. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is a GEOGRAPHICAL (physical) factor influencing population distribution?
options: Availability of water, landforms (relief), climate, and soils
The political party in power only
solution: GEOGRAPHICAL (physical) FACTORS influencing population distribution include: the AVAILABILITY of WATER (people cluster near reliable water sources — rivers, lakes); LANDFORMS/RELIEF (people prefer flat plains and gentle terrain over steep mountains); CLIMATE (moderate climates attract people, while extreme hot/cold/dry climates repel them); and SOILS (fertile soils support dense agricultural populations). These natural conditions strongly shape WHERE people can and prefer to live. So geographical factors include water, landforms, climate, and soils. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is an ECONOMIC, SOCIAL, or CULTURAL factor influencing population distribution?
options: Availability of minerals, industrialisation and urbanisation, transport, and cultural/religious significance of places
solution: ECONOMIC, SOCIAL, and CULTURAL FACTORS influencing population distribution include: the availability of MINERALS (mining areas attract population, e.g., the Copperbelt); INDUSTRIALISATION and URBANISATION (industrial and urban areas draw people seeking jobs and opportunities); TRANSPORT and connectivity (well-connected areas develop and attract population); and the CULTURAL or RELIGIOUS SIGNIFICANCE of places (e.g., religious/pilgrimage centres). These human factors, alongside physical ones, shape where people concentrate. So economic/social/cultural factors include minerals, industrialisation/urbanisation, transport, and cultural significance. So option 1 is correct.

stem: 'Population growth' (growth of population) refers to __________.
options: The change in the number of inhabitants of a territory over a specific period of time
The total area of a country
solution: POPULATION GROWTH refers to the CHANGE in the NUMBER of INHABITANTS of a territory over a SPECIFIC PERIOD of TIME (e.g., a decade). This change can be POSITIVE (increase) or NEGATIVE (decrease), and it can be expressed in absolute numbers or as a percentage/rate. Population growth is a key demographic concept, reflecting the combined effects of births, deaths, and migration. So population growth is the change in the number of people over time. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The two components of population change are __________.
options: Natural change (births minus deaths) and migration (in-migration minus out-migration)
solution: The two COMPONENTS of POPULATION CHANGE are: (1) NATURAL CHANGE — the difference between the number of BIRTHS and DEATHS (natural increase = births − deaths); and (2) MIGRATION — the movement of people, i.e., the difference between IN-MIGRATION (people moving in) and OUT-MIGRATION (people moving out). Together, natural change and net migration determine whether a population grows, declines, or stays the same. So the two components are natural change and migration. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'natural growth' of population is calculated as __________.
solution: The NATURAL GROWTH (natural increase) of population is calculated as the number of BIRTHS MINUS the number of DEATHS during a given period. If births exceed deaths, there is positive natural growth (population increase); if deaths exceed births, there is negative natural growth (decline). Natural growth reflects the population change due to biological factors alone (excluding migration). So natural growth = births − deaths. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'actual growth' of population is calculated as __________.
solution: The ACTUAL GROWTH of population is calculated by combining BOTH natural change AND migration: Actual Growth = BIRTHS − DEATHS + IN-MIGRATION − OUT-MIGRATION. In other words, it is the natural increase (births minus deaths) PLUS the net migration (in-migrants minus out-migrants). This gives the total real change in a population over a period, accounting for all the ways people are added or lost. So actual growth = births − deaths + in-migration − out-migration. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The world's population has grown very rapidly, especially __________.
options: In the last few centuries (and dramatically in the 20th century), after being relatively stable and slow-growing for most of human history
solution: The world's POPULATION has GROWN very RAPIDLY, especially in the LAST few CENTURIES — and dramatically in the 20th CENTURY. For MOST of human history, population grew very SLOWLY and was relatively STABLE (kept in check by high death rates from disease, famine, and war). Then, from around the Industrial Revolution onward, and especially in the 20th century (with advances in medicine, food production, sanitation, and technology reducing death rates), population growth ACCELERATED enormously — the so-called 'population explosion'. So world population grew rapidly especially in recent centuries and the 20th century. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rapid acceleration of world population growth in modern times is largely due to __________.
options: A sharp fall in death rates (thanks to better medicine, food supply, sanitation, and living conditions), while birth rates initially remained high
A fall in birth rates only
solution: The rapid ACCELERATION of world population growth in modern times is largely due to a SHARP FALL in DEATH RATES — brought about by better MEDICINE (vaccines, antibiotics, control of epidemics), improved FOOD SUPPLY (agricultural advances), better SANITATION and hygiene, and improved LIVING CONDITIONS — WHILE BIRTH RATES INITIALLY REMAINED HIGH. With many more people surviving (especially infants) and people living longer, but births still high, the population grew explosively. (Birth rates typically fell later, slowing growth — the demographic transition.) So the acceleration was mainly due to falling death rates while birth rates stayed high. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): Population is very unevenly distributed across the world. Reason (R): Physical factors (like water, climate, relief, soils) and human factors (like economy, transport, culture) make some areas far more attractive for habitation than others. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that population is VERY UNEVENLY distributed across the world. And the reason is (R) that PHYSICAL FACTORS (availability of WATER, favourable CLIMATE, flat RELIEF, fertile SOILS) and HUMAN FACTORS (ECONOMIC development, INDUSTRIALISATION/urbanisation, TRANSPORT, minerals, and CULTURAL significance) make SOME AREAS far MORE ATTRACTIVE for habitation than others. People cluster where conditions favour living and livelihood, and avoid harsh, resource-poor areas — which directly produces the uneven distribution (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): World population growth accelerated dramatically in the 20th century. Reason (R): Advances in medicine and technology drastically reduced death rates, so far more people survived while birth rates remained high for a time. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that world population growth ACCELERATED DRAMATICALLY in the 20th century (the 'population explosion'). And the reason is (R) that ADVANCES in MEDICINE (vaccines, antibiotics, disease control) and TECHNOLOGY (better food production, sanitation, and living standards) DRASTICALLY REDUCED DEATH RATES, so FAR MORE PEOPLE SURVIVED (especially children) and lived longer, WHILE BIRTH RATES REMAINED HIGH for a time. This large gap between high births and sharply falling deaths directly caused the population to surge (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The 'demographic transition' theory describes __________.
options: How a population's birth and death rates change over stages as a society develops (from high birth and death rates, through falling death rates, to low birth and death rates)
solution: The DEMOGRAPHIC TRANSITION theory describes HOW a population's BIRTH and DEATH RATES CHANGE over a series of STAGES as a society DEVELOPS (economically and socially). Broadly: in the first stage, both BIRTH and DEATH rates are HIGH (slow growth); in the second stage, DEATH rates FALL (due to better health/food) while birth rates stay high (rapid growth — population explosion); and in the later stage, BIRTH rates also FALL (due to development, education, family planning), so both are LOW again (slow growth or stability). The theory links demographic change to the process of development. So the demographic transition describes the change in birth/death rates through stages of development. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Roughly what share of the world's population lives in Asia?
options: About 60% (Asia is the most populous continent)
solution: ASIA is by far the MOST POPULOUS continent, home to about 60% (roughly three-fifths) of the world's population. Countries like CHINA and INDIA alone contain a very large share of humanity. This makes Asia the demographic heartland of the world. (Africa is the second most populous, followed by Europe and the Americas.) So about 60% of the world's people live in Asia. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The birth rate is defined as __________.
options: The number of live births per 1,000 people in a year
The total number of births ever
The number of deaths per 1,000 people
The number of marriages per year
solution: The BIRTH RATE (crude birth rate) is defined as the number of LIVE BIRTHS per 1,000 people in a population in a YEAR. It is a basic measure of fertility, used to compare and analyse population growth across regions and over time. (Similarly, the DEATH RATE is the number of deaths per 1,000 people per year.) So the birth rate is live births per 1,000 people per year. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The death rate is defined as __________.
options: The number of deaths per 1,000 people in a year
The number of births per year
solution: The DEATH RATE (crude death rate) is defined as the number of DEATHS per 1,000 people in a population in a YEAR. It is a basic measure of mortality. The DIFFERENCE between the birth rate and the death rate gives the rate of natural increase (or decrease) of the population. Falling death rates (with births staying high) drove the rapid population growth of modern times. So the death rate is deaths per 1,000 people per year. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Areas of very LOW population density (sparsely populated) typically include __________.
options: Hot and cold deserts, high mountains, dense equatorial forests, and polar regions
solution: Areas of very LOW population density (SPARSELY populated) typically include those with HARSH or unfavourable conditions: HOT DESERTS (e.g., Sahara) and COLD DESERTS; HIGH MOUNTAINS (steep, cold, thin air); DENSE EQUATORIAL FORESTS (hot, humid, difficult terrain, poor soils for large-scale farming); and POLAR/tundra REGIONS (extreme cold). These environments make agriculture, livelihood, and comfortable living difficult, so few people live there. (In contrast, fertile plains, industrial cities, and temperate farmlands are densely populated.) So sparsely populated areas include deserts, high mountains, dense forests, and polar regions. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The availability of fresh water is a crucial factor in population distribution because __________.
options: People need water for drinking, agriculture, industry, and daily life, so they concentrate near rivers, lakes, and other reliable water sources
solution: The availability of FRESH WATER is a CRUCIAL factor in population distribution because PEOPLE NEED WATER for DRINKING, AGRICULTURE (irrigation, crops, livestock), INDUSTRY, and DAILY LIFE. Consequently, people CONCENTRATE near reliable WATER SOURCES — especially RIVERS, LAKES, and river valleys/plains. The great river valleys (like the Ganga, Nile, Indus, and Yangtze) have historically been, and remain, among the most densely populated areas on Earth. So water availability draws population toward rivers, lakes, and reliable sources. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rate of population growth in the world has, in recent decades, begun to __________.
options: Slow down (decelerate) in many regions, as birth rates have fallen (though total population is still increasing)
solution: In RECENT DECADES, the RATE of population GROWTH in the world has begun to SLOW DOWN (decelerate) in many regions, as BIRTH RATES have FALLEN (due to development, urbanisation, education — especially of women, family planning, and changing lifestyles), following the later stage of the demographic transition. Importantly, this means the population is still INCREASING (because births still exceed deaths in most places), but at a SLOWER RATE than before. (Some developed countries have very low growth or even decline, while some developing regions still grow relatively fast.) So the growth rate has begun to slow in many regions, though total population still rises. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A 'positive' population growth means __________, and 'negative' growth means __________.
options: The population has increased (births + in-migrants exceed deaths + out-migrants); the population has decreased
The population is happy; the population is sad
There are no births; there are no deaths
The area increased; the area decreased
solution: POSITIVE population growth means the population has INCREASED over the period — i.e., additions (births plus in-migrants) EXCEED losses (deaths plus out-migrants). NEGATIVE population growth means the population has DECREASED — i.e., losses exceed additions (deaths and/or out-migration outweigh births and in-migration). Positive growth is the norm in most of the world, but some countries/regions (with very low birth rates or high out-migration) experience negative growth (decline). So positive growth = increase, negative growth = decrease. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The doubling time of a population refers to __________.
options: The number of years it takes for a population to double in size (shorter doubling times mean faster growth)
The time to build a city
solution: The DOUBLING TIME of a population refers to the number of YEARS it takes for a POPULATION to DOUBLE in SIZE at its current growth rate. A SHORTER doubling time means FASTER population growth (rapidly growing populations double quickly), while a longer doubling time means slower growth. Doubling time is a useful way to grasp the pace of population growth — for example, the world's population doubling time shortened dramatically during the population explosion. So doubling time is the years for a population to double. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): River valleys and fertile plains are densely populated. Reason (R): They offer fertile soil, water, flat land for farming and settlement, and easy transport, making them highly favourable for human habitation. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that RIVER VALLEYS and FERTILE PLAINS are DENSELY POPULATED. And the reason is (R) that they offer FERTILE SOIL (for productive agriculture), abundant WATER, FLAT LAND (easy for farming, building, and transport), and easy TRANSPORT and communication — making them HIGHLY FAVOURABLE for human habitation and livelihood. These advantages have attracted and supported dense populations in river valleys and plains (like the Ganga plain) throughout history (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): Deserts and high mountains have sparse populations. Reason (R): Their harsh conditions (extreme aridity or cold, rugged terrain, scarce water and arable land) make survival and livelihood very difficult. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that DESERTS and HIGH MOUNTAINS have SPARSE populations. And the reason is (R) that their HARSH CONDITIONS — extreme ARIDITY (deserts) or COLD (high mountains/polar areas), RUGGED terrain, and SCARCE WATER and ARABLE LAND — make SURVIVAL and LIVELIHOOD very DIFFICULT (little farming, hard living conditions, limited resources). Because these environments cannot easily support many people, they remain thinly populated (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Population density can be measured in different ways. 'Physiological density' refers to the number of people per unit of __________.
solution: PHYSIOLOGICAL DENSITY refers to the number of PEOPLE per unit of CULTIVABLE/ARABLE (cultivable) LAND — that is, the population divided by the area of land that can be used for farming, rather than the total land area. It is a more meaningful measure than simple (arithmetic) density in some contexts, because it indicates the PRESSURE of population on the productive, food-growing land. A high physiological density means many people depend on limited farmland. So physiological density is people per unit of cultivable land. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The uneven distribution of population has important implications, such as __________.
options: Concentrated demand for resources and services in dense areas, pressure on land and environment, and challenges of development and management in both crowded and empty regions
solution: The UNEVEN DISTRIBUTION of population has important IMPLICATIONS: densely populated areas face CONCENTRATED DEMAND for RESOURCES and SERVICES (food, water, housing, jobs, infrastructure), PRESSURE on LAND and the ENVIRONMENT (crowding, pollution, resource depletion), and challenges of managing large populations; while sparsely populated areas face challenges of DEVELOPMENT (providing services and infrastructure to scattered people, and utilising their resources). Understanding these patterns is essential for PLANNING and MANAGEMENT of resources, development, and the environment. So uneven distribution has implications for resource demand, environmental pressure, and development. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The study of population distribution, density, and growth is important because __________.
options: It helps in planning for resources, services, and development, and in understanding pressures on the environment and the challenges of population change
It only concerns numbers with no meaning
It is about physical geography only
solution: The study of population DISTRIBUTION, DENSITY, and GROWTH is IMPORTANT because it helps in PLANNING for RESOURCES, SERVICES (food, water, housing, education, health, jobs), and DEVELOPMENT — allocating them where people are and anticipating future needs. It also helps in UNDERSTANDING the PRESSURES that population places on the ENVIRONMENT and resources, and the CHALLENGES posed by population CHANGE (rapid growth, ageing, decline, migration). This knowledge is essential for governments, planners, and policymakers to manage human welfare and sustainability. So studying population is vital for planning, development, and environmental management. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In conclusion, the world's population can be characterised as __________.
options: Large, unevenly distributed, varying greatly in density, and dynamic (changing through births, deaths, and migration) — shaped by both natural and human factors
Concentrated in one small area only
solution: In conclusion, the world's POPULATION can be characterised as: LARGE (billions of people); UNEVENLY DISTRIBUTED (concentrated in favourable regions, sparse in harsh ones); VARYING GREATLY in DENSITY from place to place; and DYNAMIC — constantly CHANGING through BIRTHS, DEATHS, and MIGRATION (growing rapidly in modern times, though now slowing in many areas). All of this is SHAPED by BOTH NATURAL/physical FACTORS (water, climate, relief, soils) and HUMAN FACTORS (economy, industrialisation, transport, culture). This comprehensive characterisation captures the essence of the chapter. So the world's population is large, uneven, variable in density, and dynamic, shaped by natural and human factors. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The three stages of the demographic transition (in its classic form) are, in order, __________.
options: High birth and death rates (slow growth) → falling death rates with high births (rapid growth) → low birth and death rates (slow growth/stability)
Low birth rates → high death rates → no population
solution: The three classic STAGES of the DEMOGRAPHIC TRANSITION are, in order: STAGE 1 — HIGH birth rates AND HIGH death rates, so population grows SLOWLY (the pre-industrial condition); STAGE 2 — DEATH rates FALL sharply (due to better health, food, and sanitation) while BIRTH rates remain HIGH, so population grows RAPIDLY (the 'population explosion'); and STAGE 3 — BIRTH rates also FALL (due to development, urbanisation, education, and family planning), so both birth and death rates are LOW again, and population growth SLOWS or STABILISES. This model links demographic change to development. So option 1 gives the correct sequence. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In the second (expanding) stage of the demographic transition, population grows rapidly because __________.
options: Death rates fall sharply due to improvements in health, food, and sanitation, while birth rates remain high
Birth rates fall and death rates rise
solution: In the SECOND (expanding) STAGE of the demographic transition, population grows RAPIDLY because DEATH RATES FALL SHARPLY — thanks to IMPROVEMENTS in HEALTH care (medicine, vaccines, disease control), FOOD supply (agricultural advances), and SANITATION — WHILE BIRTH RATES REMAIN HIGH (social attitudes favouring large families have not yet changed). This wide GAP between still-high births and rapidly falling deaths produces a surge in population (natural increase). This stage corresponds to the 'population explosion' experienced by many developing countries. So in stage 2, falling deaths with high births cause rapid growth. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Developed countries are generally in which stage of the demographic transition?
options: The later stage — with low birth and low death rates and slow (sometimes negative) population growth
The first stage with high birth and death rates
solution: DEVELOPED countries are generally in the LATER STAGE of the demographic transition — characterised by LOW BIRTH rates and LOW DEATH rates, and therefore SLOW population GROWTH (in some cases even ZERO or NEGATIVE growth/decline, as births fall below deaths). Their development (high living standards, education, urbanisation, women's participation in work, family planning, and the high cost of raising children) has driven birth rates down to low levels. (Many developing countries, by contrast, are in the rapid-growth or transitional stages.) So developed countries are in the later, low-birth/low-death stage. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes birth rate from death rate?
options: Birth rate = live births per 1,000 people per year; Death rate = deaths per 1,000 people per year
Birth rate = deaths; Death rate = births
Birth rate = total population; Death rate = total area
solution: The correct distinction is: BIRTH RATE = the number of LIVE BIRTHS per 1,000 people per year (a measure of fertility); DEATH RATE = the number of DEATHS per 1,000 people per year (a measure of mortality). The difference between the two (birth rate minus death rate) gives the rate of natural increase. These crude rates are standard demographic measures for comparing populations. So option 1 correctly distinguishes them. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'push' and 'pull' factors are important in understanding __________.
options: Migration (push factors drive people away from a place; pull factors attract them to a new place)
solution: The 'PUSH' and 'PULL' factors are important in understanding MIGRATION — the movement of people, which is one of the components of population change. PUSH FACTORS are unfavourable conditions that DRIVE people AWAY from a place (e.g., poverty, unemployment, disasters, conflict, lack of services). PULL FACTORS are favourable conditions that ATTRACT people TO a new place (e.g., jobs, better living conditions, safety, opportunities). The interplay of push and pull factors shapes migration flows, which redistribute population. So push and pull factors relate to migration. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Migration affects population distribution by __________.
options: Decreasing the population of the areas people leave and increasing that of the areas they move to (redistributing people)
solution: MIGRATION affects population DISTRIBUTION by REDISTRIBUTING PEOPLE across space: it DECREASES the population of the areas people LEAVE (source/origin areas, through out-migration) and INCREASES the population of the areas they MOVE to (destination areas, through in-migration). Over time, migration can significantly reshape where people are concentrated — for example, rural-to-urban migration swells cities while depleting villages, and international migration changes the populations of countries. So migration redistributes population between origin and destination areas. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The largest single-country populations in the world are those of __________.
solution: The LARGEST single-country POPULATIONS in the world are those of INDIA and CHINA — the two most populous countries, each with well over a billion people, together accounting for a very large share of humanity. Both are located in Asia (the most populous continent). (India has recently become the world's most populous country, surpassing China.) So the two largest national populations are India's and China's. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Assertion (A): The rate of world population growth has started to decline in recent decades. Reason (R): Birth rates have fallen in many countries due to development, urbanisation, education (especially of women), and family planning. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the RATE of world population GROWTH has started to DECLINE in recent decades. And the reason is (R) that BIRTH RATES have FALLEN in many countries due to DEVELOPMENT, URBANISATION, EDUCATION (especially of WOMEN, which strongly lowers fertility), FAMILY PLANNING, and changing lifestyles and the higher cost of raising children. As fewer children are born per family (the later demographic-transition effect), the growth rate slows. This fall in birth rates directly explains the slowing of the growth rate (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The impact of a rapidly growing population on a country can include __________.
options: Pressure on resources, food, jobs, housing, and services; strain on the environment; but also a potentially large workforce
An automatic increase in wealth for everyone
solution: The IMPACT of a RAPIDLY GROWING POPULATION on a country can include: PRESSURE on RESOURCES, FOOD supply, JOBS, HOUSING, and public SERVICES (education, health, water, sanitation) as more people must be provided for; STRAIN on the ENVIRONMENT (land, forests, water, pollution); and challenges for development and welfare. At the same time, a large and growing population can also mean a potentially large WORKFORCE and market (a 'demographic dividend' if the working-age population is productively employed). Managing population growth to ensure it is an asset rather than a burden is a key development challenge. So rapid growth brings pressure on resources/services and the environment, alongside a potentially large workforce. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A country with a very low or negative population growth rate may face the problem of __________.
options: An ageing population and a shrinking workforce (too few young people to support the elderly and sustain the economy)
solution: A country with a VERY LOW or NEGATIVE population growth rate (as in many developed countries and, e.g., Japan and parts of Europe) may face the problem of an AGEING POPULATION and a SHRINKING WORKFORCE. With few births and longer lifespans, the proportion of ELDERLY people rises while the number of YOUNG, working-age people falls — meaning TOO FEW WORKERS to support the growing number of retirees (pensions, healthcare) and to sustain economic productivity and growth. This creates economic and social challenges (labour shortages, higher dependency burden). So low/negative growth can cause an ageing population and workforce shortage. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The distribution of population is best represented on a map using __________.
options: Dot maps (each dot representing a number of people) or density (choropleth) maps
solution: The DISTRIBUTION of POPULATION is best REPRESENTED on a MAP using techniques such as: DOT MAPS — where each DOT represents a certain NUMBER of PEOPLE, so the clustering of dots shows where population is concentrated or sparse; and DENSITY (CHOROPLETH) MAPS — where areas are SHADED according to their population DENSITY (persons per unit area). These visual methods make the spatial pattern of population (where people are crowded and where they are sparse) easy to see and analyse. So distribution is shown using dot maps and density/choropleth maps. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): About 90% of the world's people live on about 10% of the land. Reason (R): Population is concentrated in a limited number of favourable regions, while most of the Earth's surface (oceans, deserts, ice, mountains, forests) is uninhabited or thinly settled. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that about 90% of the world's PEOPLE live on about 10% of the LAND (a rough but telling statistic). And the reason is (R) that population is CONCENTRATED in a LIMITED number of FAVOURABLE REGIONS (fertile plains, river valleys, temperate and coastal areas with good conditions and economic development), while MOST of the Earth's surface — OCEANS, DESERTS, ICE-covered polar lands, high MOUNTAINS, and dense FORESTS — is UNINHABITED or thinly settled. Because habitable, attractive land is such a small fraction of the planet, the bulk of humanity crowds into it (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The factors affecting population distribution can be broadly grouped into __________.
options: Only the colour of the soil
solution: The factors affecting POPULATION DISTRIBUTION can be broadly GROUPED into two categories: (1) GEOGRAPHICAL/PHYSICAL factors — such as the availability of WATER, LANDFORMS/relief, CLIMATE, and SOILS (the natural environment's suitability for habitation); and (2) ECONOMIC, SOCIAL, CULTURAL, and POLITICAL factors — such as MINERALS, INDUSTRIALISATION and URBANISATION, TRANSPORT, economic development, and cultural/religious significance, as well as political stability and government policies. Both sets of factors together determine where people concentrate. So the factors are physical/geographical and economic/social/cultural/political. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following is an example of a place attracting population due to economic activity?
options: Mining towns, industrial cities, and commercial centres that offer jobs and opportunities
solution: Places attracting population due to ECONOMIC ACTIVITY include: MINING TOWNS (where mineral extraction offers employment, e.g., coalfields, oilfields, the Copperbelt); INDUSTRIAL CITIES (where factories and manufacturing provide jobs); and COMMERCIAL/trade CENTRES and ports (offering business and service opportunities). People migrate to and cluster in such places seeking JOBS and OPPORTUNITIES, so economic activity is a powerful pull factor concentrating population. (Empty deserts, ice caps, and barren peaks lack such opportunities and repel population.) So mining towns, industrial cities, and commercial centres attract population economically. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The 'growth of population' is significant to study because it __________.
options: Affects the demand for resources and services, the environment, the economy, and the future needs and challenges of a society
Is only a matter of curiosity
solution: The GROWTH of POPULATION is significant to study because it profoundly AFFECTS: the DEMAND for RESOURCES and SERVICES (food, water, housing, energy, education, health, jobs — more people need more of everything); the ENVIRONMENT (population pressure on land, forests, water, and pollution/climate); the ECONOMY (labour force, markets, and the balance between working-age people and dependents); and the FUTURE NEEDS and CHALLENGES of a society (planning for schools, infrastructure, ageing, etc.). Understanding population growth is therefore essential for sustainable development and policy. So studying population growth matters for resources, environment, economy, and future planning. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The relationship between population and resources is a key concern because __________.
options: A balance is needed between the number of people and the resources available to support them (over-population relative to resources can cause hardship; effective use of resources supports more people)
Population has nothing to do with resources
More people always automatically means more resources
solution: The RELATIONSHIP between POPULATION and RESOURCES is a key concern because a BALANCE is needed between the NUMBER of PEOPLE and the RESOURCES available to support them. If a population becomes too large relative to its resources (food, water, land, jobs), the result can be HARDSHIP — shortages, poverty, and environmental strain (a Malthusian concern). Conversely, with effective use of resources, technology, and management, an area can support more people. Balancing population and resources (and using resources sustainably) is thus central to human welfare and development. So the population–resource balance matters for supporting people without hardship. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The pattern of population distribution has changed over time as __________.
options: Migration, economic development, urbanisation, and technology have shifted where people live (e.g., growth of cities and industrial regions)
solution: The PATTERN of population DISTRIBUTION has CHANGED over TIME as various forces have SHIFTED where people live. MIGRATION (rural-to-urban, and between regions and countries), ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT (the rise of new industries and opportunities in particular places), URBANISATION (the rapid growth of CITIES drawing people from the countryside), and TECHNOLOGY (which allows people to live and work in areas once considered difficult) have all reshaped the distribution — for example, the growth of huge urban and industrial regions. Thus population distribution is dynamic, evolving with human activity and development. So the distribution has changed over time due to migration, development, urbanisation, and technology. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In summary, population distribution, density, and growth are governed by __________.
options: The interplay of physical environmental conditions and human (economic, social, cultural, political) factors, plus the demographic processes of births, deaths, and migration
Only the size of a country
solution: In summary, population DISTRIBUTION, DENSITY, and GROWTH are GOVERNED by the INTERPLAY of: PHYSICAL ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS (water, climate, relief, soils — determining habitability); HUMAN FACTORS (economic development, industrialisation, urbanisation, transport, minerals, culture, and political conditions — attracting or repelling people); AND the DEMOGRAPHIC PROCESSES of BIRTHS, DEATHS, and MIGRATION (which change population numbers and redistribute people over time). Together, these natural, human, and demographic forces explain where people live, how densely, and how their numbers change. So population patterns are governed by physical and human factors plus births, deaths, and migration. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The concept of 'carrying capacity' in relation to population refers to __________.
options: The maximum population that a given area/environment can support sustainably with its available resources
The weight a person can carry
The number of vehicles on a road
solution: The concept of 'CARRYING CAPACITY' in relation to population refers to the MAXIMUM POPULATION that a given AREA or ENVIRONMENT can SUPPORT SUSTAINABLY with its available RESOURCES (food, water, land, etc.) without degrading the environment or the resource base. If a population exceeds the carrying capacity, it can lead to resource depletion, environmental damage, and hardship. The idea (though carrying capacity can be raised by technology and better resource management) highlights the limits that resources place on population and the importance of balance and sustainability. So carrying capacity is the sustainable population an area's resources can support. So option 1 is correct.

stem: In conclusion, understanding the world's population is essential because __________.
options: People are the central concern of human geography, and knowing where they are, how densely they live, and how their numbers change is fundamental to planning for human welfare and sustainable development
It has no bearing on the future
solution: In conclusion, UNDERSTANDING the world's POPULATION is ESSENTIAL because PEOPLE are the CENTRAL CONCERN of human geography — human beings are both the users of the Earth and the reason for studying it. Knowing WHERE people are (distribution), HOW DENSELY they live (density), and HOW their NUMBERS CHANGE (growth) is FUNDAMENTAL to PLANNING for HUMAN WELFARE (providing food, services, jobs, and infrastructure) and for SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT (balancing population with resources and protecting the environment). This makes population study foundational to addressing the challenges of the human world. So understanding population is essential for planning human welfare and sustainable development. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth' is that:
options: Population is evenly spread and never changes

The world's population is very UNEVENLY DISTRIBUTED across the Earth (concentrated in favourable regions like South and East Asia and Europe, and sparse in deserts, mountains, forests, and polar areas), with density (persons per unit area) varying greatly — patterns shaped by PHYSICAL factors (water, climate, relief, soils) and HUMAN factors (economy, industrialisation, transport, culture); population also GROWS and changes over time through natural change (births minus deaths) and migration, and world population has grown extremely rapidly in recent centuries (especially the 20th-century 'population explosion') mainly because falling death rates (from medical and technological advances) outpaced birth rates — a process understood through the demographic transition
Population density is the same everywhere
solution: The chapter's overall message is that the world's POPULATION is very UNEVENLY DISTRIBUTED across the Earth's surface: it is CONCENTRATED in favourable regions (such as SOUTH and EAST ASIA — India, China — and EUROPE and north-eastern USA), while VAST areas (deserts, high mountains, dense forests, and polar regions) are SPARSELY populated. POPULATION DENSITY (the number of persons per unit area, e.g., per square km) therefore varies GREATLY from place to place. These patterns of distribution and density are SHAPED by PHYSICAL/geographical factors (availability of WATER, favourable CLIMATE, flat RELIEF, fertile SOILS) and by HUMAN factors (ECONOMIC development, MINERALS, INDUSTRIALISATION and URBANISATION, TRANSPORT, and CULTURAL/religious significance). Population is not static but GROWS and CHANGES over time, through two components: NATURAL CHANGE (BIRTHS minus DEATHS) and MIGRATION (in-migration minus out-migration) — with actual growth combining both. The chapter emphasises that world population has grown EXTREMELY RAPIDLY in recent centuries — especially the 20th-century 'POPULATION EXPLOSION' — MAINLY because FALLING DEATH RATES (thanks to advances in MEDICINE, food supply, sanitation, and living standards) OUTPACED birth rates for a time, a process understood through the DEMOGRAPHIC TRANSITION model (the change in birth and death rates through stages of development). So the overall message is option 2.
